pairs.question: I really want to quit smoking, but I feel like cigarettes are my best friends. What should I do?
pairs.answer: One thing you can do is to list your reasons for wanting to quit and review them during the quitting period. It’s also important to make plans for how to deal with problems you will encounter before you quit.
pairs.evidence: One thing that you can do is to list your reasons for wanting to quit and review them during the quitting period. Making plans for how to deal with problems you will encounter before you quit is important.

pairs.question: What should I think about when I want to quit smoking?
pairs.answer: Think about what triggers you to smoke and what you can do instead of lighting a cigarette at those times. Changing your routines and rituals associated with smoking will also be necessary.
pairs.evidence: Think about what triggers you to smoke and what you can do instead of lighting a cigarette at those times. Think about the routines and rituals associated with your smoking that you will need to change during the process of quitting.

pairs.question: I feel like this is a bad time for me to quit smoking because I'm so busy and stressed. Should I wait?
pairs.answer: Using tobacco doesn't help with stress; it just relieves nicotine withdrawal symptoms. Once you are tobacco-free, your stress levels will eventually fall below what they were as a stressed-out tobacco user.
pairs.evidence: Using tobacco doesn't help with stress. It just relieves the nicotine withdrawal symptoms when you haven't used tobacco for a while.

pairs.question: I smoke low tar/nicotine cigarettes. Are they actually healthier for me?
pairs.answer: People who use low tar/nicotine cigarettes smoke more and inhale more deeply to compensate for low nicotine levels. They end up getting the same tar/nicotine levels as they would with higher tar/nicotine brands.
pairs.evidence: People who use low tar/nicotine cigarettes smoke more cigarettes and inhale more often and more deeply to compensate for low nicotine levels in these cigarettes.

pairs.question: What should I do if I feel irritable when I try to quit smoking?
pairs.answer: There are a number of medications that can help to reduce withdrawal symptoms. Talk to your healthcare provider about available choices.
pairs.evidence: There are a number of medications that can help to reduce the withdrawal symptoms. Talk to your healthcare provider about available choices.

pairs.question: Is it normal to feel stressed when trying to quit smoking?
pairs.answer: Yes, it's common to use tobacco when things get tough because of your dependence on nicotine. But once you quit, your stress levels will improve.
pairs.evidence: It is common to use tobacco when things get tough because of your dependence on nicotine.

pairs.question: How can I manage my stress while trying to quit smoking?
pairs.answer: Once you are tobacco-free, your stress levels will eventually fall below what they were as a stressed-out tobacco user. Quitting can lead to better stress management.
pairs.evidence: Once you are tobacco-free your stress levels will eventually fall below what they were as a stressed-out tobacco user.

pairs.question: I feel like I need to smoke to cope with my stress. Is that true?
pairs.answer: It's a common misconception. Using tobacco just relieves withdrawal symptoms, not stress. Quitting can actually help reduce your stress in the long run.
pairs.evidence: Using tobacco doesn't help with stress. It just relieves the nicotine withdrawal symptoms when you haven't used tobacco for a while.

pairs.question: Will I gain weight if I stop smoking?
pairs.answer: Many tobacco users gain weight when they quit, but it is usually less than 10 pounds. It's best not to diet right away; focus on quitting first.
pairs.evidence: Many tobacco users gain weight when they quit, but it is usually less than 10 pounds.

pairs.question: Can exercise help me when I quit smoking?
pairs.answer: Exercise is an effective technique to help cope with withdrawal symptoms and life stress. It can also help reduce weight gain.
pairs.evidence: Exercise is an effective technique to help cope with withdrawal symptoms and life stress and also to help reduce weight gain.

pairs.question: Do I need to worry about nicotine levels in low tar cigarettes?
pairs.answer: People often compensate for low nicotine levels in low tar cigarettes, ending up with the same tar/nicotine levels as higher tar/nicotine brands.
pairs.evidence: They end up getting the same tar/nicotine levels as they would with higher tar/nicotine brands.

pairs.question: What should I avoid when I first stop smoking?
pairs.answer: Avoid high-calorie snacks when you first stop smoking. You can focus on dieting later when you're an established nonuser.
pairs.evidence: Avoid high-calorie snacks. Exercise is an effective technique to help cope with withdrawal symptoms and life stress and also to help reduce weight gain.

pairs.question: Can medications help with weight gain when quitting?
pairs.answer: Some medications to help you quit may limit weight gain while you are taking them. It's worth discussing with your healthcare provider.
pairs.evidence: Some of the medications to help you quit may limit weight gain while you are taking them.

pairs.question: Should I tell my friends and family that I'm trying to quit smoking?
pairs.answer: Yes, you should enlist family, friends, and coworkers who would be supportive. Having a support system can really help!
pairs.evidence: Yes. You should enlist family, friends and coworkers who would be supportive.

pairs.question: I tried to quit cold turkey but only lasted two days. What should I do?
pairs.answer: It's common to struggle with quitting cold turkey. Talk to your healthcare provider about different medications that can help reduce withdrawal symptoms.
pairs.evidence: When you do decide to quit, talk to you healthcare provider about different medications that can help to reduce withdrawal symptoms.

pairs.question: What kind of withdrawal symptoms should I expect when I quit smoking?
pairs.answer: You might experience symptoms like nervousness, light-headedness, sleep disturbances, fatigue, and cravings. It's all part of the process.
pairs.evidence: Some other physical and psychological withdrawal symptoms are nervousness, light-headedness, sleep disturbances, fatigue, constipation, mouth sores, headache, hunger, depression, and cravings.

pairs.question: I thought quitting snuff would be easy, but I only lasted two days. Is that normal?
pairs.answer: It's actually quite common to struggle with quitting. Smokeless tobacco is as addictive as smoked tobacco, heroin, and cocaine, so it's understandable that quitting can be tough.
pairs.evidence: Smokeless tobacco is as addictive as smoked tobacco, heroin, and cocaine.

pairs.question: What should I do if I want to quit using smokeless tobacco?
pairs.answer: When you're ready to quit, talk to your healthcare professional about referring you to a helpline. They can also discuss some smokeless tobacco alternatives and medications that might help you quit.
pairs.evidence: When you are ready to quit, talk to your healthcare profession about referring you to a helpline and discuss some smokeless tobacco alternatives and medications that might be helpful to help you quit.

pairs.question: I feel like I can't quit on my own. Is there support available?
pairs.answer: Yes, there is support available! Your healthcare professional can refer you to a helpline that specializes in helping people quit smokeless tobacco.

pairs.question: Are there medications that can help me quit smokeless tobacco?
